title: Transfer Functions
description: Describe how a circuit scales and shifts each frequency component with H(f) = V_out/V_in.

study.title: Signals are sums of sinusoids
study.body: Fourier analysis shows that practically any signal can be written as a sum of sinusoids with different frequencies, amplitudes and phases. A **periodic** signal with period $T$ contains only a dc term plus components at the fundamental $f_0 = 1/T$ and its harmonics $2f_0, 3f_0, \ldots$ Non-periodic signals such as speech have components spread over a continuous range (audio: roughly 20 Hz to 15 kHz).
study.formula: v(t) = V_0 + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} V_n\cos(2\pi n f_0 t + \theta_n)

study.title: The transfer function
study.body: A **filter** is a two-port circuit that changes the amplitude and phase of each component depending on its frequency. For a sinusoidal input of frequency $f$, the transfer function is the output phasor divided by the input phasor. It is complex: $|H(f)|$ is the ratio of output to input amplitude and $\angle H(f)$ is the phase shift the filter adds.

study.title: Output for one sinusoid
study.body:
Read the frequency from the input ($f = \omega/2\pi$), evaluate $H$ at that frequency and multiply phasors: **magnitudes multiply, angles add**. The output has the same frequency as the input.
**Example:** $H(500\text{ Hz}) = 2\angle{-30^\circ}$ and $v_{in}(t) = 3\cos(1000\pi t + 10^\circ)$ V give $V_{out} = 2\angle{-30^\circ} \times 3\angle 10^\circ = 6\angle{-20^\circ}$, so $v_{out}(t) = 6\cos(1000\pi t - 20^\circ)$ V.

study.title: Inputs with several components
study.body:
Use superposition and treat each component on its own:
- split the input into components; note each frequency and phasor
- evaluate $H(f)$ at each frequency (a dc term is the component at $f = 0$, multiplied by the real number $H(0)$)
- multiply to get each output phasor
- convert each output phasor back to a time function and **add the time functions**
Never add phasors of different frequencies.

study.title: Finding H(f) from a circuit
study.body: Replace every element by its impedance ($R$, $j2\pi fL$, $1/(j2\pi fC)$) and solve for $V_{out}/V_{in}$, usually with a voltage divider. To measure $H(f)$, apply a sinusoid, record the amplitudes and phases of input and output in steady state, divide, and repeat for each frequency of interest. Beware: $H(f)$ depends on the load connected to the output.

steps.title: Signals as sums of sinusoids
steps.body: Fourier analysis tells us that almost any signal is a sum of sinusoids. A periodic signal with period $T$ has a dc part plus components at $f_0 = 1/T$ and its **harmonics** $2f_0, 3f_0, \ldots$
steps.formula: v(t) = V_0 + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} V_n\cos(2\pi n f_0 t + \theta_n)

steps.prompt: A periodic voltage repeats every $T$ = {{T|s}}. At which frequencies can it contain sinusoidal components?
steps.explanation: The fundamental frequency is $f_0 = 1/T$ = 1/{{T|s}} = {{1/T|Hz}}. A periodic signal can only contain a dc term and harmonics at integer multiples of $f_0$: {{1/T|Hz}}, {{2/T|Hz}}, {{3/T|Hz}}, … Values like $2\pi/T$ are angular frequencies in rad/s, not frequencies in Hz.

steps.title: The transfer function
steps.body: A **filter** passes some frequency components and weakens others. For a sinusoidal input of frequency $f$, its transfer function is the output phasor divided by the input phasor. $|H(f)|$ tells how much the amplitude is scaled, $\angle H(f)$ how much the phase is shifted.

steps.prompt: At the input frequency a filter has $|H(f)| = 0.5$ and $\angle H(f) = -60^\circ$. The output sinusoid then has half the input amplitude and lags the input by 60°.
steps.explanation: $V_{out} = H\,V_{in}$: the amplitude is multiplied by 0.5 and −60° is added to the phase. A negative phase shift means the output reaches its peaks later, so it lags the input by 60°.

steps.title: Output for one sinusoid
steps.body: For an input $A\cos(\omega t + \theta)$ the frequency is $f = \omega/2\pi$. Evaluate $H$ at that frequency and multiply phasors: **magnitudes multiply, angles add**. The output has the same frequency as the input.

steps.prompt: The input is $v_{in}(t) = 5\cos({{k}}\pi t)$ V. At which frequency $f$ must you evaluate $H(f)$?
steps.explanation: $\omega$ = {{k}}π rad/s, so $f = \omega/2\pi$ = {{k}}π/(2π) = {{k/2|Hz}}. Answering {{k|Hz}} forgets the factor 2; {{k*pi|Hz}} confuses the angular frequency (rad/s) with the frequency (Hz).

steps.prompt: At {{f|Hz}} a filter has $H = {{Hm}}\angle{{th}}^\circ$. The input is $v_{in}(t) = {{A}}\cos(2\pi\cdot{{f}}\,t + {{ph}}^\circ)$ V. What is the amplitude of $v_{out}(t)$?
steps.explanation: Magnitudes multiply: $V_{out,m} = |H|\,V_{in,m}$ = {{Hm}} × {{A|V}} = {{A*Hm|V}}. (The phase becomes {{ph}}° + ({{th}}°) = {{ph+th}}°, and the frequency stays {{f|Hz}}.)

steps.prompt: At {{f|Hz}} a filter has $H = {{Hm}}\angle{{th}}^\circ$ and the input is $v_{in}(t) = {{A}}\cos(2\pi\cdot{{f}}\,t + {{ph}}^\circ)$ V. Writing $v_{out}(t) = V_m\cos(2\pi\cdot{{f}}\,t + \theta)$, find $\theta$ in degrees.
steps.explanation: Angles add when phasors are multiplied: $\theta = \theta_{in} + \angle H$ = {{ph}}° + ({{th}}°) = {{ph+th}}°. The output amplitude is {{Hm}} × {{A}} = {{A*Hm|V}}.

steps.prompt: The graph shows the input $v_{in}$ (grey, dashed) and the output $v_{out}$ (solid) of a filter at one frequency. What does the filter do at this frequency?
options: It attenuates the signal and the output lags ($\angle H < 0$)
It amplifies the signal and the output lags ($\angle H < 0$)
It attenuates the signal and the output leads ($\angle H > 0$)
It amplifies the signal and the output leads ($\angle H > 0$)
steps.explanation: Magnitude: compare the peaks. The input peak is 1 V and the output peak {{g}} V, so $|H| = V_{out}/V_{in}$ = {{g}}: below 1 the filter attenuates, above 1 it amplifies. Phase: the input peaks at $\omega t$ = 0° and 360°, the output at {{mod(-ph,360)}}°. An output peak that comes **later** than the matching input peak means a lag ($\angle H < 0$), an earlier one a lead. Here $\angle H$ = {{ph}}°.

steps.prompt: A filter has $H(f) = \frac{K}{1 + jf/f_c}$ with $K$ = {{K}} and $f_c$ = {{fc|Hz}}. Find $|H(f)|$ at $f$ = {{f|Hz}}.
steps.explanation: The magnitude of a quotient is the quotient of magnitudes: $|H| = \frac{K}{\sqrt{1 + (f/f_c)^2}}$. Here $f/f_c$ = {{f/fc}}, so $|H|$ = {{K}}/√(1 + {{(f/fc)^2}}) = {{K/sqrt(1+(f/fc)^2)}}.

steps.prompt: A filter has $H(f) = \frac{K}{1 + jf/f_c}$ with $K$ = {{K}} and $f_c$ = {{fc|Hz}}. Find the phase $\angle H(f)$ at $f$ = {{f|Hz}}, in degrees.
steps.explanation: Phase of a quotient = phase of numerator − phase of denominator. The numerator $K$ is real and positive (0°); the denominator $1 + j${{f/fc}} has angle $\arctan$({{f/fc}}) = {{deg(atan(f/fc))}}°. So $\angle H$ = {{-deg(atan(f/fc))}}°.

steps.prompt: The input $v_{in}(t) = {{V0}} + {{A1}}\cos(2\pi\cdot{{f1}}\,t)$ V is applied to a filter with $H(0) = {{H0}}$ and $H({{f1}}\text{ Hz}) = {{H1}}\angle{{t1}}^\circ$. What is the dc component of $v_{out}(t)$?
steps.explanation: The dc term is a component at $f = 0$, so it is multiplied by $H(0)$: $V_{out,dc}$ = {{H0}} × {{V0|V}} = {{V0*H0|V}}. The {{f1|Hz}} component is handled separately: it becomes a sinusoid with amplitude {{A1*H1|V}} and phase {{t1}}°.

steps.prompt: A filter has $H(0) = {{H0}}$, $H(1\text{ kHz}) = {{H1}}\angle{-20^\circ}$ and $H(3\text{ kHz}) = {{H2}}\angle{-75^\circ}$. The input is $v_{in}(t) = {{V0}} + {{A1}}\cos(2000\pi t) + {{A2}}\cos(6000\pi t)$ V. Find the amplitude of the 3 kHz component of $v_{out}$.
steps.explanation: $6000\pi t$ means $f = 6000\pi/2\pi$ = 3 kHz, so use $H(3\text{ kHz})$: amplitude = {{H2}} × {{A2|V}} = {{A2*H2|V}} (phase −75°). The other components use their own $H$ values and are added as separate time functions.

steps.prompt: At 500 Hz a filter has $H = {{Ha}}\angle{{ta}}^\circ$, at 1500 Hz $H = {{Hb}}\angle{{tb}}^\circ$. For $v_{in}(t) = {{A}}\cos(1000\pi t) + {{B}}\cos(3000\pi t + 20^\circ)$, which is $v_{out}(t)$?
steps.explanation: $1000\pi t$ is the 500 Hz component and $3000\pi t$ the 1500 Hz one. 500 Hz: {{A}}∠0° × {{Ha}}∠{{ta}}° = {{A*Ha}}∠{{ta}}°. 1500 Hz: {{B}}∠20° × {{Hb}}∠{{tb}}° = {{B*Hb}}∠{{20+tb}}°. Convert each back to a cosine and add the time functions. Subtracting the angles, or using the wrong frequency's $H$, are the typical mistakes.

steps.prompt: Put the steps for finding a filter's output for a multi-frequency input in order.
items: Split the input into components; note each frequency and phasor
Evaluate H(f) at each component's frequency
Multiply each input phasor by its H(f)
Convert each output phasor back to a time function
steps.explanation: This is superposition: each frequency passes through the filter independently. Phasors of different frequencies cannot be added, so the components are converted to time functions before adding.

steps.prompt: To measure $H(f)$ at {{f|Hz}}, you see on an oscilloscope that each output peak occurs {{dt|s}} **after** the corresponding input peak. What is $\angle H(f)$ in degrees (between −180° and 0°)?
steps.explanation: One period is $T = 1/f$ = {{1/f|s}}. A delay of {{dt|s}} is {{frac}} of a period, i.e. {{frac}} × 360° = {{360*frac}}°. The output lags, so $\angle H$ = −{{360*frac}}°.

steps.prompt: The graph shows one period of the input $v_{in}$ (grey, dashed) and the output $v_{out}$ (solid) of a filter.

ask.explanation: The input peaks at $t = 0$ and $t = T$ = {{T|s}}; the output peaks at $t$ = {{dt|s}}, a fraction {{dt/T}} of a period. $\angle H = \theta_{out} - \theta_{in} = -360^\circ\cdot t_{peak}/T$ = {{-360*dt/T}}°, which is the same angle as {{ph}}° (a later peak is a lag, a negative angle).

steps.prompt: Which expression is the transfer function $H(f) = V_{out}/V_{in}$ of this circuit?
options: $\frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2 + j2\pi f C R_1 R_2}$
$\frac{R_1}{R_1 + R_2 + j2\pi f C R_1 R_2}$
steps.explanation: $R_2$ and $C$ are in parallel: $Z_p = \frac{R_2}{1 + j2\pi f C R_2}$. Voltage divider: $H = \frac{Z_p}{R_1 + Z_p} = \frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2 + j2\pi f C R_1 R_2}$. Dividing through by $R_1 + R_2$ gives $H = \frac{K}{1 + jf/f_B}$ with $K = \frac{R_2}{R_1+R_2}$ and $f_B = \frac{1}{2\pi C (R_1\|R_2)}$. Ignoring $R_2$ or putting $R_1$ in the numerator are the typical slips.

steps.prompt: The input of this circuit is $v_{in}(t) = {{V0}} + 2\cos(2000\pi t)$ V. What is the dc component of $v_{out}(t)$?
steps.explanation: At $f = 0$ the capacitor is an open circuit, so $H(0) = \frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2}$ = {{R2|Ω}}/({{R1|Ω}} + {{R2|Ω}}) = {{R2/(R1+R2)}}. The dc output is {{R2/(R1+R2)}} × {{V0|V}} = {{V0*R2/(R1+R2)|V}}.

steps.prompt: For this circuit, find $|H(f)| = |V_{out}/V_{in}|$ at $f$ = {{f|Hz}}.
steps.hint: Write H(f) = K/(1 + jf/f_B) with K = R₂/(R₁+R₂) and f_B = 1/(2πC(R₁∥R₂)).

steps.prompt: For this circuit, find the phase $\angle H(f)$ at $f$ = {{f|Hz}}, in degrees.
steps.explanation: $H = \frac{K}{1 + jf/f_B}$ with real $K$, so $\angle H = -\arctan(f/f_B)$. $R_1\|R_2$ = {{par(R1,R2)|Ω}} gives $f_B$ = {{fB|Hz}}, so $f/f_B$ = {{f/fB}} and $\angle H$ = {{-deg(atan(f/fB))}}°.

steps.prompt: At low frequencies this circuit has $|H| = R_2/(R_1+R_2)$. At what frequency has $|H|$ dropped to $1/\sqrt{2}$ of that value?
steps.explanation: $|H| = K/\sqrt{1 + (f/f_B)^2}$ equals $K/\sqrt 2$ when $f = f_B$. The capacitor sees the Thévenin resistance $R_1\|R_2$ = {{par(R1,R2)|Ω}}, so $f_B = \frac{1}{2\pi C(R_1\|R_2)}$ = 1/(2π × {{C|F}} × {{par(R1,R2)|Ω}}) = {{1/(2*pi*C*par(R1,R2))|Hz}}.

steps.prompt: The circuit is driven by $v_{in}(t) = 3 + {{A}}\cos(2\pi\cdot{{f}}\,t)$ V. Find the amplitude of the sinusoidal part of $v_{out}(t)$.
steps.explanation: Only the {{f|Hz}} component matters here. $K$ = {{K}}, $f_B$ = {{fB|Hz}}, so $|H({{f}}\text{ Hz})|$ = {{K}}/√(1 + {{(f/fB)^2}}) = {{K/sqrt(1+(f/fB)^2)}}. Amplitude = {{K/sqrt(1+(f/fB)^2)}} × {{A|V}} = {{A*K/sqrt(1+(f/fB)^2)|V}}. (The dc part separately becomes 3 × {{K}} = {{3*K|V}}.)

steps.prompt: If you connect a load resistor across the output terminals of this circuit, its transfer function $H(f)$ stays the same.
steps.explanation: The load appears in parallel with $R_2$ and $C$, changing $Z_p$ and therefore both $K$ and $f_B$. A transfer function is only valid for the load it was derived (or measured) with — the same reason $H_1$ of a cascade must be found with the next stage attached.
